description:
We are a team of ambitious Math & Computer Science students who are really looking forward to developing a viable software in aid of current NASA liabilities.

Currently we specialize in Data Analysis, Discrete Math & Algorithms. These are directly correlated to our selected challenge, which involves path-finding using Martian data.
summary:
ARES-Nav is a Mars exploration and route-planning tool developed for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It brings terrain, rover imagery, exploration sites, and atmospheric context together in a tactical map of Gale and Jezero craters. Users can choose a starting point and destination, inspect terrain hazards, and generate routes using a slope-aware pathfinding algorithm that estimates distance, travel time, and elevation change.

The project addresses the challenge by turning planetary and rover data into a human-scale planning interface for future astronauts, helping them consider both scientific targets and hazards before an EVA. It is important because crews on Mars would need clear, localized information to make decisions with limited real-time support from Earth.
details:
ARES-Nav is an interactive tactical map for planning Mars surface explorations at Gale and Jezero craters. Users can inspect a 3D view of the terrain, explore rover imagery and mission waypoints, review hazards, and select route endpoints. A slope-aware pathfinding algorithm searches a terrain-cell graph for a traversable route and reports estimates such as distance, travel time, and elevation change. The interface also presents atmospheric and EVA resource context to help users think through the conditions and trade-offs of an expedition.

The project brings planetary data into a human-scale planning experience: instead of viewing terrain, imagery, and hazards separately, explorers can consider them together when choosing a route and science targets. We designed it around the needs of future crews operating far from Earth support, prioritizing readable hazard cues, interactive exploration, and practical route estimates. The result is intended as a decision-support concept—not a certified operational or safety system.

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js for the interactive map and 3D visualization. The Python backend provides API services and terrain analysis, using tools including NumPy, SciPy, and NetworkX for data processing and route calculations. The project draws on NASA Mars imagery, rover waypoints, and terrain products. Gale’s 3D relief model is bundled locally and georeferenced against MOLA/HRSC data; Jezero’s route slopes use a supplied HiRISE raster, while its elevation terrain is procedural demonstration data. We considered data resolution, map usability, hazard visibility, estimated traversal effort, and the limitations of incomplete or simulated data.
